**Choose C and use the fallback desk for one refused complex case.** The provider accepts all six routine cases and one complex case: they use all nine effort units and yield the provider its greatest profit under C. Provider payments are $16. The fallback desk confirms one of the two refused complex cases for $3, bringing the result to **8 confirmed cases for $19**.

For comparison, A leads the provider to accept only the six routine cases; fallback brings the total to 7 for $15. Under B, accepting a complex case adds no profit, so the tie rule makes the provider choose only the six routine cases. Fallback would raise spending to $21, above the ceiling, leaving B at 6 confirmations for $18.

The dashboard shows 100% confirmation among accepted cases, but omits refusals. Under C, it hides the two refused complex cases: the provider confirms 7 of all 9 registered arrivals, and fallback brings the buyer’s total to 8 of 9. The buyer remains responsible for the one unresolved refusal.

Choose **C** and use the fallback desk for one refused complex case. The provider accepts all six routine cases and one complex case: that uses all nine effort units and gives it the greatest profit under C. Provider payments are \(6 \times \$2 + 1 \times \$4 = \$16\). Fallback adds one confirmed resolution for $3, bringing the result to **8 of 9 cases confirmed for $19**.

Under A, the provider accepts only the six routine cases; fallback brings the total to 7 for $15. Under B, it also accepts only the six routine cases: complex cases add no profit, so the tie rule excludes them. Those six confirmations cost $18, leaving too little for fallback.

The dashboard would show **100% confirmation for the seven cases the provider accepted under C**. It omits the two registered refusals. The full registry shows eight confirmations after fallback and one unresolved complex case for which the buyer remains responsible.

**Choose C and use the fallback desk for one refused complex case.** The provider accepts all six routine cases and one complex case, using all nine effort units. Its profit is $7; no other feasible subset gives it more. Provider payments are $16, and fallback costs $3, so the buyer spends **$19** for **eight customer-confirmed resolutions**. The remaining complex case is refused and remains the buyer’s responsibility.

The dashboard shows 100% confirmation because every *accepted* case is confirmed. It omits the two refusals. The clerk’s registry shows the full nine-case picture: eight confirmed after fallback, one unresolved.
